nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
June 15, 1994. Douglas Marvin Scheidt; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
September 20, 1996.  R.G. Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

Common Name:  Atlantic Thread Herring
Scientific Name: Opisthonema oglinum

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Clupeiformes
	Family: Clupeidae

Other Common Names: Hairyback, shad herring, bristle herring.

Other: References for scientific name include (Lesueur 1817; 2303; 2329; 1914)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  The Atlantic thread herring is an under exploited fish, that is abundant in the Gulf of Mexico and is mainly caught as an incidental catch in the menhaden fishery (2331).  Several times a fishery has been attempted to target this species but, have failed due to low demand and marketability.
Recreational: Atlantic thread herring is used as bait in the recreational fishery (2329).
Ecological Role:  Clupeids represent one of the greatest sources of harvestable live animal protein in tropical seas, the biology of these fishes is important (2313).   Reintjes (1979) stated that thread herring is an important prey species that is eaten by a variety of carnivorous fish, sea birds, and marine mammals (2329).  Atlantic thread herring were documented as prey for herons (851) and for mackerel (2328) and seatrout, snapper and mackerel (2313).
Indicator:  None known

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Principally a tropical species with extralimital occurrence to the Gulf of Maine. Found to Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico, Puerto Rico and the Caribbean (2329; 2341; 2326). In Florida found on the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts (2338; 2334; 2331; 848; 993; 2337; 2322).
Within Study Area:  Found within the Indian River Lagoon near ocean inlets (848; 993; 2337) and on the adjacent continental shelf (848; 2322).
Mobility and Migration:
Life Mode:  A schooling planktivorous coastal pelagic tropical species found usually in water less than 90-150 m in depth.
Migrations and Movements:  During the winter Atlantic thread herring concentrate in shallow waters between St. Petersburg and Ft. Meyers (2334).  Thread herring move in advance of the 20 C (68 F) isotherm (2334).  Atlantic thread herring can migrate on a seasonal north-south tract on the Gulf coast of Florida and stay within the territorial boundaries of the state (2334).  On the Atlantic coast, thread herring migrate to the south in the winter months, with an average movement of 6 to 7 miles per day or up to a total of 370 miles (2338).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Atlantic thread herring prefer shallow coastal waters usually less than 35 m in depth, with most schools found in water less than 11 m in depth (2329).  In the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, Atlantic thread herring have been found in neritic, surf zone reefs, surf zone sand, inlets and grass flats (848; 993).  The Atlantic thread herring can inhabit all portions of the water column but, concentrate in the upper 3 m (2334).   Juveniles in Biscayne Bay are found in seagrass beds from April to early winter (2313).
Substrate:  Shallow coastal waters
Physical/Chemical:  Temperature - Tropical or subtropical in temperature preference (2329).  Found in water temperatures of 26-29 C but, absent in temperatures below 17 C and at temperatures above 29 C (2334; 2341; and 2329).  In the winter as temperatures reach below 20 C migrations start toward warmer waters (2334; 2341).

nodes.title: WATER COLUMN HABITAT
nodes.body:
Salinity:  Adults found in high salinities 32 - 34 ppt (2334; 2341; 2329).  Juveniles have been found in salinities as low as 5 ppt in estuarine waters (2329).
Temperature:  Most eggs and larvae less than 5 mm were taken in temperatures above 25 C and surface salinity above 25 ppt (2331).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, Iteroparous, Oviparous, Broadcast spawner, Polygamous.
Mating and Spawning:   In the Gulf of Mexico, eggs have been collected from March through September with peak egg collections occurring May through August (2332; 2331).   Spawning usually takes place within 50 km of shore in shallow water less than 30 m (2331).  The highest concentration of eggs collected occur in the coastal waters between St. Petersburg and Ft. Meyers where data suggest that a large portion of thread herring population remains year round in this area (2331).  On the Atlantic coast spawning was documented during February through June and in August (2322).  Spawning frequency is not well known, some researchers indicate that thread herring may be multiple spawners in northwest Florida, while in Biscayne Bay, Low (1973) found spawning as early as March-April, Martinez (1972) found one primary modal group (2329) wereas, Houde and Lovdal (1984) found two peaks in the spring. In Brazil (2336) found they spawn only once a year.  Newly fertilized eggs collected only at night (2331).
Fecundity:  Fecundity ranges from 13,638 to 50,339 eggs with a mean of 30, 922 eggs (2329)

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Fertilized eggs are buoyant (2304).   Egg diameter ranges from 1.10-1.28 mm with a mean of 1.19 mm (2340).  Embryos can make up to 59% of the egg diameter in the blastodisc stage (2340).    Eggs can hatch in less than 24 hrs in water temperatures 25-30 C in the Gulf of Mexico (2331).    Houde (1977) extrapolated hatching time from data showing that newly fertilized eggs were found at night 2200-0200 hrs and full term embryos were found only in the afternoon of the next day 1400-1800 hrs.
Larvae: Size ranges from 3.8 mm NL to 19.3 mm SL (2304).
Juvenile:   Juvenile stage begins at 19.7 mm SL (Jones et al 1978).   The mean growth rate of larvae is 0.8 mm per day.  Mortality from spawning to 15.5 mm SL can be as great as 99 % or as few as 6 larvae per 1000 spawned eggs reach 15.5 mm SL (2331).  Juveniles found in seagrass beds from April to early winter (2313).
Adult: Specimens mature as small as 135 mm SL (2304).  Males reach maturity at a smaller size with males maturing at 125 mm FL and females at 145 mm FL (2327).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Copepods dominate as the major food item other items include; pelecypods, gastropods and "cypris" stage of barnacles, there is also evidence of some bottom feeding and carnivorous feeding (2330; 98).  Kinch (1979) found no particular food item dominated but, rather a diet of non-selective benthic grazing with a high proportion of mud and organic debris found in the gut.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Reintjes (1979) stated that thread herring is an important prey species that is eaten by a variety of carnivorous fish, sea birds, and marine mammals (2329).  Atlantic thread herring were documented as prey for herons (Sogard et al. 1990) and for mackerel (2328) seatrout, snapper and mackerel (2313).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Atlantic Thread Herring (Opisthonema oglinum)

FLELMR CODE: 1169

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
June 15, 1994. Douglas Marvin Scheidt; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
September 20, 1996.  R.G. Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

Common Name:  Atlantic Thread Herring
Scientific Name: Opisthonema oglinum

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Clupeiformes
	Family: Clupeidae

Other Common Names: Hairyback, shad herring, bristle herring.

Other: References for scientific name include (Lesueur 1817; 2303; 2329; 1914)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  The Atlantic thread herring is an under exploited fish, that is abundant in the Gulf of Mexico and is mainly caught as an incidental catch in the menhaden fishery (2331).  Several times a fishery has been attempted to target this species but, have failed due to low demand and marketability.
Recreational: Atlantic thread herring is used as bait in the recreational fishery (2329).
Ecological Role:  Clupeids represent one of the greatest sources of harvestable live animal protein in tropical seas, the biology of these fishes is important (2313).   Reintjes (1979) stated that thread herring is an important prey species that is eaten by a variety of carnivorous fish, sea birds, and marine mammals (2329).  Atlantic thread herring were documented as prey for herons (851) and for mackerel (2328) and seatrout, snapper and mackerel (2313).
Indicator:  None known

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Principally a tropical species with extralimital occurrence to the Gulf of Maine. Found to Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico, Puerto Rico and the Caribbean (2329; 2341; 2326). In Florida found on the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts (2338; 2334; 2331; 848; 993; 2337; 2322).
Within Study Area:  Found within the Indian River Lagoon near ocean inlets (848; 993; 2337) and on the adjacent continental shelf (848; 2322).
Mobility and Migration:
Life Mode:  A schooling planktivorous coastal pelagic tropical species found usually in water less than 90-150 m in depth.
Migrations and Movements:  During the winter Atlantic thread herring concentrate in shallow waters between St. Petersburg and Ft. Meyers (2334).  Thread herring move in advance of the 20 C (68 F) isotherm (2334).  Atlantic thread herring can migrate on a seasonal north-south tract on the Gulf coast of Florida and stay within the territorial boundaries of the state (2334).  On the Atlantic coast, thread herring migrate to the south in the winter months, with an average movement of 6 to 7 miles per day or up to a total of 370 miles (2338).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Atlantic thread herring prefer shallow coastal waters usually less than 35 m in depth, with most schools found in water less than 11 m in depth (2329).  In the Indian River Lagoon and adjacent waters, Atlantic thread herring have been found in neritic, surf zone reefs, surf zone sand, inlets and grass flats (848; 993).  The Atlantic thread herring can inhabit all portions of the water column but, concentrate in the upper 3 m (2334).   Juveniles in Biscayne Bay are found in seagrass beds from April to early winter (2313).
Substrate:  Shallow coastal waters
Physical/Chemical:  Temperature - Tropical or subtropical in temperature preference (2329).  Found in water temperatures of 26-29 C but, absent in temperatures below 17 C and at temperatures above 29 C (2334; 2341; and 2329).  In the winter as temperatures reach below 20 C migrations start toward warmer waters (2334; 2341).

sections.heading: WATER COLUMN HABITAT
sections.content:
Salinity:  Adults found in high salinities 32 - 34 ppt (2334; 2341; 2329).  Juveniles have been found in salinities as low as 5 ppt in estuarine waters (2329).
Temperature:  Most eggs and larvae less than 5 mm were taken in temperatures above 25 C and surface salinity above 25 ppt (2331).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, Iteroparous, Oviparous, Broadcast spawner, Polygamous.
Mating and Spawning:   In the Gulf of Mexico, eggs have been collected from March through September with peak egg collections occurring May through August (2332; 2331).   Spawning usually takes place within 50 km of shore in shallow water less than 30 m (2331).  The highest concentration of eggs collected occur in the coastal waters between St. Petersburg and Ft. Meyers where data suggest that a large portion of thread herring population remains year round in this area (2331).  On the Atlantic coast spawning was documented during February through June and in August (2322).  Spawning frequency is not well known, some researchers indicate that thread herring may be multiple spawners in northwest Florida, while in Biscayne Bay, Low (1973) found spawning as early as March-April, Martinez (1972) found one primary modal group (2329) wereas, Houde and Lovdal (1984) found two peaks in the spring. In Brazil (2336) found they spawn only once a year.  Newly fertilized eggs collected only at night (2331).
Fecundity:  Fecundity ranges from 13,638 to 50,339 eggs with a mean of 30, 922 eggs (2329)

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Fertilized eggs are buoyant (2304).   Egg diameter ranges from 1.10-1.28 mm with a mean of 1.19 mm (2340).  Embryos can make up to 59% of the egg diameter in the blastodisc stage (2340).    Eggs can hatch in less than 24 hrs in water temperatures 25-30 C in the Gulf of Mexico (2331).    Houde (1977) extrapolated hatching time from data showing that newly fertilized eggs were found at night 2200-0200 hrs and full term embryos were found only in the afternoon of the next day 1400-1800 hrs.
Larvae: Size ranges from 3.8 mm NL to 19.3 mm SL (2304).
Juvenile:   Juvenile stage begins at 19.7 mm SL (Jones et al 1978).   The mean growth rate of larvae is 0.8 mm per day.  Mortality from spawning to 15.5 mm SL can be as great as 99 % or as few as 6 larvae per 1000 spawned eggs reach 15.5 mm SL (2331).  Juveniles found in seagrass beds from April to early winter (2313).
Adult: Specimens mature as small as 135 mm SL (2304).  Males reach maturity at a smaller size with males maturing at 125 mm FL and females at 145 mm FL (2327).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Copepods dominate as the major food item other items include; pelecypods, gastropods and "cypris" stage of barnacles, there is also evidence of some bottom feeding and carnivorous feeding (2330; 98).  Kinch (1979) found no particular food item dominated but, rather a diet of non-selective benthic grazing with a high proportion of mud and organic debris found in the gut.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Reintjes (1979) stated that thread herring is an important prey species that is eaten by a variety of carnivorous fish, sea birds, and marine mammals (2329).  Atlantic thread herring were documented as prey for herons (Sogard et al. 1990) and for mackerel (2328) seatrout, snapper and mackerel (2313).
